title: “‘Other Mommy’ Tops Box Office; ‘Social Reckoning’ Vanishes, ‘Verity’ & ‘Resident Evil’ Surge”
body:
Universal’s latest horror entry, “Other Mommy,” is on pace to claim the No. 1 spot at the domestic box office with a projected $28 million opening weekend, according to the latest weekend‑by‑weekend estimates. The film, which opened in 3,365 theaters on Friday, has quickly out‑performed its competition, while the much‑buzzed‑about documentary “The Social Reckoning” appears set to land at No. 5 with an estimated $6 million haul. Meanwhile, a slate of genre‑leaning releases—including “Verity,” “Resident Evil: Nice Holds,” and the long‑running adventure “The Odyssey”—have all secured places inside the top‑10, underscoring a weekend that favoured familiar franchises and horror‑driven fare.

“Other Mommy” benefits from a perfect storm of factors that have traditionally propelled horror movies to strong openings. The film’s marketing campaign leaned heavily on social‑media teasers and a series of immersive “playdate” events that allowed audiences to experience key set pieces in pop‑up installations across major cities. Those efforts translated into solid per‑theater averages, with many venues reporting near‑full capacity during the first two days. Industry analysts point to the film’s blend of psychological tension and visceral scares as a fresh take on the “mother‑monster” sub‑genre, a niche that has seen renewed interest after the success of titles like “The Babadook” and “Midsommar.” The $28 million forecast, while still shy of the $45 million opening recorded by last year’s horror blockbuster “The Haunting of Hill House,” marks the strongest debut for a Universal horror picture this calendar year.

In contrast, “The Social Reckoning,” a documentary that delves into the rise and impact of social‑media platforms, is expected to bring in roughly $6 million, positioning it at No. 5. The film’s modest earnings reflect a crowded market for nonfiction titles and a limited theatrical rollout—only 1,200 screens nationwide. Nevertheless, its presence in the top five highlights a growing appetite for socially relevant content, especially among younger demographics who are increasingly seeking out stories that examine the digital landscape they inhabit. Critics have praised the documentary’s investigative depth, but its box‑office performance suggests that streaming will remain the primary distribution channel for this genre.

The weekend’s top‑10 also featured “Verity,” a psychological thriller that opened to $12 million, and “Resident Evil: Nice Holds,” the latest entry in the long‑standing video‑game adaptation franchise, which pulled in $9 million. Both films benefited from strong fan bases and strategic release dates that avoided direct competition from major summer blockbusters. “The Odyssey,” the adventure epic that has been lingering in the upper‑mid tier of the chart for several weeks, added $5 million to its cumulative total, buoyed by a resurgence of interest following a recent award‑season buzz campaign. The diversity of genres—horror, thriller, sci‑fi, and adventure—demonstrates the current box‑office landscape’s reliance on established IPs and genre loyalty rather than original, high‑budget spectacles.

Analysts note that the weekend’s numbers underscore a broader trend: as studios navigate a post‑pandemic environment, they are increasingly hedging bets on mid‑budget genre films that can deliver solid returns with relatively modest marketing spends. Universal’s confidence in “Other Mommy” reflects a strategic pivot toward horror, a genre that historically offers high profit margins due to lower production costs and strong fan engagement. Meanwhile, the modest showing of “The Social Reckoning” may encourage distributors to prioritize hybrid release models, pairing limited theatrical runs with rapid streaming availability to capture both box‑office revenue and digital viewership.

Looking ahead, the performance of “Other Mommy” will set the tone for the next wave of horror releases slated for the fall, including several sequels and original concepts slated for October. If the film maintains its momentum, it could not only secure a profitable run for Universal but also reinforce the studio’s commitment to expanding its horror slate. For “The Social Reckoning,” the upcoming awards season could provide a second wind, potentially boosting its streaming numbers and cementing its place as a cultural touchstone on the conversation around social media. As audiences continue to gravitate toward familiar franchises and genre comfort, the coming weeks will reveal whether studios can sustain this model or if a breakout original will reshape the box‑office hierarchy.
